clue.text: Secret of success in an oral examination ?

definitions.text: Secret of success in an oral examination

parts.words: Secret of success in an oral examination
parts.note: the oral examination is a sentry's challenge, passed by saying the agreed secret word

explanation.surface: A student wonders what wins a viva voce.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a viva at university; the 'examination' is a sentry's challenge, where the secret word spoken aloud lets you through.
explanation.definitionFit: A sentry admits only those who give the agreed secret word, so it is literally the key to passing a spoken test.

clue.text: The beak 'shows spirit when' kept up

explanation.surface: A judge looks lively in court.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The beak' looks like slang for a magistrate; here it is a bird's bill. 'Keep your pecker up' is British slang for stay cheerful.
explanation.definitionFit: A bird's bill is what it pecks with; to keep one's courage up is the idiom with the same word.

clue.text: You, can't' claim, this without good reason

definitions.text: You, can't' claim, this without good reason

parts.words: You, can't' claim, this without good reason
parts.note: good reason is soundness of mind, so claiming mental health requires having it

explanation.surface: A lawyer warns that a claim needs justification.
explanation.walkthrough: 'good reason' means justification in the surface; read it as a sound mind.
explanation.definitionFit: Soundness of mind is having one's reason in good order.

clue.text: A considerable drop of moisture

parts.note: a drop here is a fall in height, not a droplet, and a big one taken by water

explanation.surface: A large bead of water forms.
explanation.walkthrough: 'drop' suggests a droplet; it is a descent, a big one made by water.
explanation.definitionFit: A cascade is river water plunging a long way down a cliff.

clue.text: AAA directors attached to their vintage car?

definitions.text: AAA directors attached to their vintage car?

parts.words: AAA directors attached to their vintage car?
parts.note: the AAA is the Amateur Athletic Association, whose governing body would be a board for running

explanation.surface: Motoring club officials love their old automobile.
explanation.walkthrough: AAA suggests a motoring club; the Amateur Athletic Association's directors form a board for running. Old cars had a step along the side by that name.
explanation.definitionFit: Old cars had a footboard along the side, and athletics directors are a board for runners.

clue.text: A pill if taken the wrong way can stimulate

indicators.note: read in the wrong direction, so the run of letters in these two clue words is turned backwards

explanation.surface: A tablet swallowed awkwardly might give someone a jolt.
explanation.walkthrough: 'taken the wrong way' turns PILLIF, the letters of 'pill if', backwards; 'A' and 'can' are link words.
explanation.definitionFit: As a verb, to fillip is to give a boost or spur, which is to stimulate.

clue.text: I had become attached to Manxland, in a manner of speaking

parts.note: I had contracts to I'd
Manxland is the Isle of Man, abbreviated IOM

explanation.surface: A newcomer settles happily on the Isle of Man.
explanation.walkthrough: 'become attached to' joins the pieces. The Isle of Man is a British crown dependency in the Irish Sea.
explanation.definitionFit: An idiom is a set expression peculiar to a language, a turn of phrase.

clue.text: Terribly cruel set of instructions

indicators.note: terribly suggests the letters are badly mangled, signalling an anagram

explanation.surface: A harsh list of orders is issued.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Terribly' rearranges CRUELSET; 'of' is a link word.
explanation.definitionFit: Lectures are talks that teach, a form of instruction.

clue.text: Why is a padre disguised here ?

indicators.note: disguised means the letters appear in a different form, an anagram

explanation.surface: A puzzled observer wonders why a chaplain is wearing a costume.
explanation.walkthrough: 'disguised' rearranges ISAPADRE. 'here' is the place a good padre hopes to end up.
explanation.definitionFit: Heaven is where a priest expects to go, so 'here' points to that place.

clue.text: "But I am —— as the northern star" (J. Caesar).

definitions.text: But I am —— as the northern star" (J. Caesar).

parts.words: But I am —— as the northern star" (J. Caesar).
parts.note: a quotation with a word blanked out: Caesar compares his steadfastness to the Pole Star, which never moves

explanation.surface: Caesar boasts of his firmness in Shakespeare's play.
explanation.walkthrough: The page prints a blank after 'am'; the full line in Julius Caesar is 'But I am constant as the northern star'. Supply the missing word.
explanation.definitionFit: The Pole Star keeps its place in the sky, an image of unchanging steadfastness.

clue.text: One that delivers the meat chop-chop?

definitions.text: One that delivers the meat chop-chop?

parts.words: One that delivers the meat chop-chop?
parts.note: chop-chop means quickly, as if for a speedy delivery man, but here the meat is delivered chopped into pieces

explanation.surface: A butcher's boy hurries round with the joints.
explanation.walkthrough: 'chop-chop' reads as slang for 'hurry up', but the kitchen gadget delivers meat in chopped-up form.
explanation.definitionFit: A kitchen grinder pushes meat out finely chopped.

clue.text: Partners in crime? If resisting' union membership was' one

definitions.text: If resisting' union membership was' one

explanation.surface: Accomplices are compared to a rebel who fought the trade union.
explanation.walkthrough: 'union' looks like a trade union; it is the Union of the American Civil War, resisted by the southern states.
explanation.definitionFit: Accomplices are allies in wrongdoing; the southern states that fought the Union were the allied rebels of the Confederacy.

clue.text: Samson's enigmatic source of meat

parts.note: Samson's riddle in Judges 14 runs 'Out of the ... came forth meat', meaning honey found in a lion's carcass

explanation.surface: A Bible riddle asks where the food came from.
explanation.walkthrough: Samson's riddle: 'Out of the eater came forth meat, and out of the strong came forth sweetness', the honey in the dead lion.
explanation.definitionFit: In the riddle the lion, a devourer, is the source from which food came.

clue.text: Stain on oil-drum, perhaps

indicators.note: perhaps suggests the letters might be arranged some other way, signalling a rearrangement

explanation.surface: A mark appears on a metal barrel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'perhaps' asks for an anagram of ON OILDRUM, nine letters, giving the rust stain.
explanation.definitionFit: Iron mould is a rust or ink mark left on cloth, a type of stain.

clue.text: Used by gunners or by those who seek the mountains?

explanation.surface: Artillerymen and mountaineers share a piece of kit.
explanation.walkthrough: Read the answer as a phrase for the second sense: people looking for a mountain range.
explanation.definitionFit: Artillery crews measure distance to targets with optical instruments; climbers hunting a chain of peaks are seekers of a range.

clue.text: Hugo wrote one over this number

definitions.text: Hugo wrote one over this number

parts.words: Hugo wrote one over this number
parts.note: Victor Hugo's last novel is named for a year number; the answer is one less than that number

explanation.surface: A French novelist went over his word count.
explanation.walkthrough: Victor Hugo wrote 'Quatrevingt-treize', Ninety-three; one over the answer gives that title.
explanation.definitionFit: The novel's title number exceeds this number by exactly one.

clue.text: They have no legal right to their 'takings

definitions.text: They have no legal right to their 'takings

parts.words: They have no legal right to their 'takings
parts.note: takings suggests shop money, but these people seize thrones or power without lawful claim

explanation.surface: Shopkeepers are accused of keeping money unlawfully.
explanation.walkthrough: 'takings' looks like a shop's cash; it means what is seized, such as a throne.
explanation.definitionFit: Those who seize power wrongfully hold it without any lawful title.

clue.text: "The fairest of her ——s Eve" (Milton)

parts.note: a line from Paradise Lost with one word blanked out, describing Eve among her female descendants

explanation.surface: A quotation praises the first woman's beauty.
explanation.walkthrough: The page prints a blank plus s; Milton's line is 'the fairest of her daughters Eve', so the blank takes the singular.
explanation.definitionFit: Milton calls Eve the loveliest of all the women born after her, her female offspring.

clue.text: Wouldn't one get a good grip of farming here ?

definitions.text: Wouldn't one get a good grip of farming here

parts.words: Wouldn't one get a good grip of farming here
parts.note: a modest plot of farmland is read as a little hold, the kind of grip a hand might take

explanation.surface: Someone asks where best to learn agriculture.
explanation.walkthrough: 'grip' points to a hold, and a small farm is a small holding.
explanation.definitionFit: A modest farm plot is a little piece of land that is held, giving a hands-on grasp of agriculture.

clue.text: Bumper numbers

parts.note: in Oxford bumping races boats chase and bump each other, and the crews take their name from the number of rowers

explanation.surface: Bumper numbers suggests large quantities.
explanation.walkthrough: In Oxford and Cambridge 'bumps' races, crews of that many rowers try to bump the boat in front.
explanation.definitionFit: College rowing crews of that size take part in bumping races.

clue.text: Prominent figure in a pop song

definitions.text: Prominent figure in a pop song

parts.words: Prominent figure in a pop song
parts.note: the nursery rhyme 'Pop goes the ...' features an animal, the pop of the title

explanation.surface: A star appears in a chart hit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'pop song' suggests chart music; it is the rhyme 'Pop goes the weasel'.
explanation.definitionFit: The animal in the old song title is the one that goes pop.

clue.text: Grit's rare, causing trouble in a recorder

indicators.note: these letters are stirred up and thrown into disorder, signalling an anagram

parts.note: the possessive s is kept here as a letter

explanation.surface: Uncommon sand jams a tape machine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'causing trouble' rearranges GRITSRARE; the 's of 'Grit's' supplies the S. 'recorder' is a person, not a device.
explanation.definitionFit: An official who keeps the register of births, marriages and deaths is a keeper of records.

clue.text: Trophy of victory, for the brave

definitions.text: Trophy of victory, for the brave

parts.words: Trophy of victory, for the brave
parts.note: 'brave' as a noun is a Native American warrior, who took a piece of the enemy's head as a prize

explanation.surface: A medal awaits the courageous.
explanation.walkthrough: 'the brave' reads as courageous people; here a brave is a Native American warrior.
explanation.definitionFit: Warriors took the skin of a defeated foe's head as proof of the kill.

clue.text: Instant cereal after tea say?

indicators.note: after places the cereal following the tea
say signals that the word before it is to be heard, so tea is spoken as its sound

parts.note: tea sounds like the letter T
rice is a cereal grain

explanation.surface: Quick-cook grains follow a cuppa.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Instant cereal' looks like a packet of breakfast food; 'Instant' is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: In a trice means in a moment, so the noun is a brief instant.

clue.text: 'Cricketers "don't always have to run for them

definitions.text: Cricketers "don't always have to run for them

parts.words: Cricketers "don't always have to run for them
parts.note: runs added to the score not off the bat, such as wides, no-balls and byes, sometimes come without running

explanation.surface: A batsman is grateful for some free runs.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket, wides and no-balls add runs to the total without the batsmen having to run.
explanation.definitionFit: Runs credited to the team that are not scored off the bat are counted as bonus additions to the score.

clue.text: Not that, the comedian at the nudist camp would have us in these

definitions.text: Not that, the comedian at the nudist camp would have us in these

parts.words: Not that, the comedian at the nudist camp would have us in these
parts.note: to be in fits of laughter is an idiom; at a nudist camp no clothes need sewing, so only the laughing sense applies

explanation.surface: A stand-up performs to naked holidaymakers.
explanation.walkthrough: The joke: nobody at a nudist camp wears sewn garments, but a comic might still leave the audience helpless with laughter.
explanation.definitionFit: Being 'in' these means laughing uncontrollably; they are also the threads of sewing, absent from naked campers.

clue.text: Athletic pursuits turn into instruments of sharp practice

indicators.note: turn into says the letters are converted into a new form, an anagram

parts.note: athletic pursuits are sports

explanation.surface: Games are converted into tools for cheating.
explanation.walkthrough: 'turn into' rearranges SPORTS. 'sharp practice' suggests cheating, but strops literally keep razors sharp.
explanation.definitionFit: Barbers hone razors on leather straps, so they are tools for practising sharpness.

clue.text: Marriage with a cause ?

parts.note: one can wed a person or take up a cause, and the same word covers both acts of commitment

explanation.surface: A campaigner seems married to their mission.
explanation.walkthrough: The word means both a wedding and the adopting of a cause.
explanation.definitionFit: The noun covers a betrothal or wedding and also embracing a belief or movement.
